drafts.title: Hypothetical Batching: Aggregate Throughput vs. Batch Size (Illustrative)
drafts.body:
This post explores a hypothetical scenario concerning batch processing for local LLMs, explicitly stating that no actual measurements were taken. The core question is how aggregate throughput might change with varying batch sizes.

In this hypothetical experiment, a batch size of 1 was associated with an aggregate throughput of 22 tokens per second. Increasing the batch size to 4 in this scenario hypothetically yielded an aggregate throughput of 55 tokens per second.

It is crucial to note that these figures are purely illustrative and do not represent real-world test results. The observed rates are aggregate values, not per-request metrics. Furthermore, per-request latency was not assessed in this hypothetical setup. These numbers are intended solely to prompt discussion on the potential tradeoffs between batch size and overall processing capacity in local LLM deployments, acknowledging the hypothetical nature of the data.

drafts.title: Illustrative Throughput: Batch Size 4 vs. Batch Size 1 in Hypothetical LLM Processing
drafts.body:
Considering a hypothetical scenario for local LLM processing, we can examine potential impacts of batching on aggregate throughput. It's important to preface this discussion by stating that the following figures are illustrative and not derived from actual tests or measurements.

In this hypothetical model, a batch size of 1 resulted in an aggregate throughput of 22 tokens per second. By comparison, a batch size of 4 in the same hypothetical test yielded an aggregate throughput of 55 tokens per second. These values are intended to provoke thought about scaling processing by increasing batch size.

Key limitations must be highlighted: these are aggregate rates, not individual request speeds, and per-request latency was not a measured variable. The data presented is synthetic and serves only to frame a discussion around the theoretical benefits of batching for overall throughput in local LLM applications, while explicitly maintaining its hypothetical status.
